Question: If there is no God, how do atheists explain how the moon is perfectly circular?
Answer: Your ignorance is showing, Luis Aguilar. It’s unsightly… please cover it up. The Moon is not “perfectly circular”. A circle is a two-dimensional geometric construct. The Moon exists in three linear dimensions which, like the Earth, is an oblate spheroid. The explanation is trivial: it’s gravity. The only gravitationally stable shape for large objects in space is roughly the sphere. Matter in a collection falls toward the center of gravity. In a sphere, all matter forms equidistant from the center of gravity. Any other shape and you’d have things still falling toward the center, as long as the object is large enough and not acted on by other forces. The actual shape, whether it’s oblate — flattened along an axis — depends on such other forces, such as rotation, tidal friction, and the gravitational effect of other bodies. You might be so uneducated you invoke deities to explain things that humanity in collective has known for thousands of year, like some bronze age gothsherd. But don’t expect the rest of civilization to sink to your level just because you’re too stupid or lazy to learn grade-school science. Read More

Question: If you are obese, at what age do you believe you will die? Seeing as there aren't many 70+ year olds walking around morbidly obese.
Answer: This guy’s morbidly obese — it’s technically called Class III obesity — though he tries to dress in ways that cover it up (edit: he’s not really Class III — some people can’t take a joke — but he’s been obese and likely Class II for some time, though in fairness, he might have lost weight since leaving office). He’s also really famous — I’m thinking you know about him — and he’ll be 78 in two months. I’m not sure I’ve seen him walking very often, but standing, sitting, and particularly, golf carting, absolutely! You can find any number of lifespan calculators if you’re concerned about longevity, but there are any number of contributing factors. It seems that the guy shown above, given what’s know about his current health, could live to 82–85 years old. But the devil is always in the details, and while this man’s father lived to 93 — pretty good — he suffered from Alzheimer’s Dementia for a decade and eventually succumbed to the disease. Why don’t you normally see obese people in their 70s? It depends on many things. How many morbidly obese people younger than 70 do you normally come across in your average day? It’s easy to imagine having a lifestyle that filters them out. I’m out with my dog 2–4 miles a day… it’s pretty unlikely I’m going to meet too many obese folks when I’m out walking. It takes a particular lifestyle, and sometimes an unfortunate medical condition, to get like that. I also don’t see them too often when cycling or kayaking, but I do see them occasionally at the beach. And now and then in the grocery store, but I don’t got to those all that often. I also don’t eat out all that often, and when I do, it’s not low quality food. I’m not claiming that all obese people eat at McDonald’s or Golden Corral, but one of the contributing factors toward obesity is eating too much poor quality food… Hamburders! And the typical Golden Corral customer is a regular, over 65, and in the USA, they live in the south. The last time I ate out was at the VFW in Madeira Beach, FL… wasn’t crowded, and I didn’t notice anyone terribly overweight. And as well, do you see folks in their 70s on a regular basis? They’re another group that doesn’t necessarily intersect yours on a regular basis. Most at that age are retired, and many retirees leave their former business-friendly locales for something nicer and/or with lower cost of living. In short, you can’t build a useful statistical model about 70+ obese people, or anyone else, just noticing who you meet in your everyday life. Yes, obesity is a leading long-term cause of health issues. It’s a contributing factor to many things that kill you: dementia, heart disease, diabetes, cancer, osteoarthritis, high blood pressure, gallbladder disease, fatty liver disease, and breathing problems like asthma and sleep apnea. But obesity alone doesn’t just kill you when you turn 70. In fact, according to the CDC, 41.5% of Americans aged 60 and older have at least Class I obesity. That’s not all that different than the 39.8% of Americans 20–39 who are obese. So maybe you didn’t know it, but statistically, about four out of every ten people you pass on average in the USA are obese. Maybe some of them are over 70, and maybe you didn’t notice either thing. Are you a trained medical professional? Or maybe this is just so common, only extreme obesity stands out. That statistic alone does tell you that there are lots of fat old people still walking around. And while I mentioned Class III obesity, your question was targeted at any sort of obesity. It’s common being overweight in a prosperous country that revels in junk food and sedentary activities. In fact, I could stand to lose 10lbs… maybe I’ll take the dog out four miles this evening! Self-reflection is always a good thing, eh? CRITICAL UPDATE We went 3.92 miles yesterday, 2.74 today. The weather was perfect.

Name: Dave Haynie
Question: Why do my iPhone pictures look better than pictures taken from my DSLR camera?
Answer: Q: Why do my iPhone pictures look better than pictures taken from my DSLR camera? The bottom line here is that your phone is a better photographer than you are. Seriously… but read on. The fact you can pick up a smartphone and take pretty good photos but are struggling with the DSLR should tell you that you’re missing some understanding of photography. So, let’s consider the iPhone. As a camera, this is the distant descendant of the Kodak Instamatic. Seriously. The Instamatic was designed as a camera for people who had no idea how to take photos. There was nothing to set, your option was basically: flash bulb or no flash bulb. It had a fixed lens, fixed aperture, fixed shutter speed, and that’s that. It worked as well as it did because Kodak got some crazy exposure latitude out of their processing. Anyway, the idea was simple: point, shoot, and you love your photos. Even though they were usually pretty awful! The iPhone is the modern embodiment of this idea: point, shoot, love your photo. It is made for someone with absolutely not a clue about photography. It’s not even a camera, it’s a pocket-sized personal computer with more power than your desktop computer had 10 years ago, and more AI processing power than your present desktop/laptop might offer today. About six or so years ago, companies like Google and Apple started throwing that weight behind their cameras. They didn’t want to increase expenses, they didn’t want to make fatter phones — they ultimately did both in an effort to one-up last year’s models, and each other — but the key with smartphones has been computational and artificial intelligence hardware and software. Not as much the camera sensor. Last I checked, your iPhone is constantly shooting while you run the Camera app. It’s using an AI agent to set exposure, another to set focus, and and maybe one to decide exactly when to shoot. I know Google does that in low light. It keeps 8 photos in memory in a circular buffer. When you press the shutter icon, the shooting stops… usually. That’s why it seems to be instant… the photos are already taken! In bright light, it’ll pick the best of four sets of two. It’s alternating exposures for HDR. In lower light it’ll try to use all eight, and in very low light, it’ll take another long (and probably blurry) photo to try to learn about the color in the scene, because these little sensors don’t get good color in low light at high ISO to avoid blur and shake. There’s an AI agent to direct these things, to merge color, etc. Then there’s another AI agent to decide how to “finish” the image, kind of like using a Preset in Lightroom but certainly more involved, since the AI has to pick the appropriate look. Apple wants to deliver a photo you’ll like, but they don’t give too much concern about realism. Though maybe a bit more than Samsung, who seem to want all their photos so saturated you’ll think you shot them in Oz or Candyland or something. Anyway, my point is that Apple, in particular, is doing all of the work. Not you. They have a network of AI agents that function together to replace the need for a photographer, or more specifically, a photographer’s brain. With an experienced photographer, it’s not the camera. Any camera will do, in part because you’ll make it work, and shoot different images depending on the limitations and advantages of that particular camera gear. If you’re blaming anything on the camera, you don’t understand photography… or you’re using a smartphone, which isn’t allowing you the control you want. Understand that there’s always better in photography, but in the digital age, pretty much any camera made from 2012 on is sufficient to not be your problem. One quick lesson: one way to get to this kind of understanding is to limit yourself. Folks did this with P&S cameras, and they did with older smartphones. But now with all their fake zoom and multiple cameras, smartphones can make you as lazy as DSLRs sometimes do. So try it simple. You should be out and around, shooting photos every week at the least, every day that you can. So take a week or a month, pick one prime lens, maybe turn off the automation (though manual focus is difficult on most DSLRs) and just shoot with that lens, nothing else. In fact, my Olympus Pen-F is sitting here on the desk with a few hundred photos taken with just one 25mm f/0.95 manual lens last Sunday. The single most important component of a camera is the twelve inches behind it! -Ansel Adams There is nothing worse than a sharp image of a fuzzy concept. -Ansel Adams Read that. Understand it. If you are not getting better shots with your DSLR, it’s because you haven’t learned how to get better shots with your DSLR. Period. It’s not the camera. Sure, you can always get a better lens. Then maybe you’ll have a sharper bad photo than you do today. The single best investment in photography anyone can buy once the put down a smartphone and pick up a dedicated camera is knowledge. A serious camera isn’t made for smartphone users, at least not yet, people who don’t know what they’re doing. It’s made as a tool for those who do, and the digital innovations offered in DSLRs and even more in mirrorless cameras are designed to be used and useful to experienced photographers, not novices without any real camera experience. Don’t get me wrong, you learn some creative aspects of photography with a smartphone. Not everything, but the creative side, sure. But you’re not normally controlling focus, you can’t really control depth of field (yeah, they fake it a bit… it’s not the same), you’re not learning to control light if you’re just snapshooting. You’re finishing (editing) your photos and learn what’s entailed in all of that. And it’s not just you. I have seen dozens of video done in perfect seriousness, in which a supposedly experienced photographer is proving that his iPhone or Samsung or whatever can out-shoot him (and yeah, so far, it’s always a dude). If you understand what you’re doing, it’s pretty easy to watch one of these and see immediately what the guy is doing wrong… often it’s just assuming that AUTO mode with a DSLR makes you an expert and that it can match the trillions of AI cycles tossed at AUTO mode on a smartphone. It can’t, and it isn’t even trying. What AUTO on a real camera does is act very, very consistently, which makes it a tool a photographer can use. I’m always in control, even if I set the dial on “P” … which is pretty rare. So, grasshopper, once you can see this too, you are ready to talk about camera gear. Until then, learning is your road to success. You may also not be exercising your photo chops. Taking great photos with a real camera requires practice and regular attention just like painting, just like playing the guitar, just like wood carving, etc. You don’t expect a guitar to play itself, and you don’t blame the guitar if you sound choppy or keep missing chords. You blame yourself. That’s not chastising, it’s accepting the fact that you have more learning to do, and that should be what drew you to photography. In short, any money you’re spending on photography at this point needs to be on learning. I know, it’s so much more work than buying that shiny new lens that half the people here are suggesting you might need. They’re wrong. Learn to be a photographer. That can be lessons online, that can be local classes, and in both cases it needs to be getting out and shooting. Give yourself a project! I decided to produce a B&W photo every day… I did that for 1,000 days. I learned a whole lot about B&W photography in the digital age. I got better, even after 35+ years of prior experience going back to my darkroom as a kid. This is also the edge professionals have: they’re immersed fulltime in the work… well, aside from the other full-time job they have running the business. The negative is the score, and the print is the performance. -Ansel Adams You don’t take a photograph, you make it. -Ansel Adams Dodging and burning are steps to take care of mistakes God made in establishing tonal relationships. -Ansel Adams So, yes, in the days of the darkroom, dodging and burning — the old way of “editing an image” — to create a great print was very much a performance. Today, you have Lightroom, Photoshop, and other tools with “undo” buttons, etc. So while it’s not precisely a performance anymore, it’s still as much a part of making a great image as the shooting is. Particularly for some kinds of photography. True, you have street photography and photojournalism that may rely more heavily on the lightly or unedited image, but if it’s at all art, the finishing, the print matters too. Of course, while we may not be making prints all the time, we’re still releasing a photographs on some kind of medium, even if it’s just a JPEG on Quora. Understanding the result you want is a big part of being able to get satisfaction from shooting. One of the great things about editing, however you do it, is that it lends itself to a whole creative experimentation that’s simply not available if you’re just point-and-shooting. Here’s one example. When I was shooting this at City Hall in Philadelphia, I knew immediately that there was too much contrast in the scene to capture this in one shot. So I composited this by hand. Maybe your camera’s or phone’s HDR function would have captured it, maybe it wouldn’t have. I knew with basic exposure bracketing that I’d nail it, so there was no worry, and I had full control over the final image. So here’s what I started with. Even if the iPhone could capture the dynamic range, is it really going to keep a full tonal range, etc? I’m kind of wondering if there’s so much AI in some of these phones, is it really my image anymore when I see it? And how much longer until it’s not? Here’s another somewhat challenging shot as finished, one of my favorites from my B&W project. This was only a single shot, and taken awfully quickly. This is a default version of the raw image. Now, if a smartphone AI image processor got hold of this, it would look better. In fact, there would likely not be much in the way of shadow areas at all… but that’s actually an important part of the finished image. One more. I shot this in Philadelphia. I liked the interesting look of this old building, and knew it would be a nice B&W image. Of course, I shot in raw from street level, and when you do that with a wide lens, your building tilts backwards. I knew this, of course, and I actually could have applied keystone correction in-camera. But I didn’t bother, I knew Photoshop would offer me more control and not bake any edits into the image. Yeah, technically, I could have done both. Whether your smartphone could do any of this for you is kind of moot… it’s not as much my work if the smartphone gets to make creative decisions. Yes, these are things you can and should learn to do yourself. Learn to use a camera, learn creative photography, learn the “digital darkroom” and you will outshoot your smartphone. Ultimately, only you can decided “best” between images. And that’s another thing: look at other folks photography. That’s part of learning. I mention the great Ansel Adams here because, as a kid, I was obsessed with the outdoors and especially the National Parks. I was also shooting, processing, and printing my own B&W film, and it was seeing Adams’ prints in person that made me really fall in love with B&W and darkroom work. Just knowing that was possible, even if I had no idea how he did it! Read More

Question: Can you focus a lens manually on a mirrorless camera?
Answer: Absolutely, at least on any of the commonly available mirrorless ILC systems. On some camera/lens combinations, you’ll have to explicitly set manual focus mode. Some cameras have an AF+MF mode. In this mode, you’re shooting in autofocus until you use the focus ring, then you’re in manual, probably for the duration of the shot (but know your system). Sometimes there’s an auto/manual switch on the lens or camera body. Yeah, that’s a DSLR in the image, a Nikon D7100, not a mirrorless model, but there’s nothing especially different in auto/manual focus controls on mirrorless, DSLR, and point-and-shoot cameras. Sometimes it’s a focus ring clutch… slide the focus ring back to reveal the distance scale, and you’re in manual focus. Push it forward to hide the distance scale and you’re in auto focus. Mirrorless cameras are also easy to use with manual lenses. The mirrorless viewfinder is brighter and lends itself to more accurate “focus by eye” than that of most DSLRs. Plus, you can switch in focusing aids like focus peaking or magnification. Your EVF will also compensate if you’re using a manual aperture lens stopped down, boosting brightness to make it easier to compose your shot.

Question: Should the practice of burning religious books be banned and made illegal?
Answer: I don’t personally approve the burning of any books. That’s my opinion. Yours may well be different. The fundamental problem I have is that the practice of burning books is a signal that those burning them consider the contents to be dangerous thoughts and ideas. That one person or a group of people think some ideas are dangerous does not make them so. They may simply be trying to suppress those ideas for their own reasons… maybe they represent a competing idea. But even if they are in some way dangerous, I think dangerous thoughts and ideas are not only important but necessary for societal growth. Decisions about society made decades or centuries ago should be regularly challenged against the backdrop of modern times. Such ideas deserve their chance to compete in the marketplace of ideas, to succeed or fail on their own merit. Not be quashed via any violent suppression. Yes, even religious books, despite the fact I think they’re all rather silly. Unlike some people, I openly acknowledge it’s not all about me. That’s not the same as saying that I believe book burning should be illegal. There are sound reasons why book burning of any kind isn’t and can’t be made illegal: Of course, I’m speaking in terms of US Law. There are countries that don’t respect individual freedom and unusually protect religion — or more likely, only some religion — via things like blasphemy laws. Under those regimes, burning certain religious texts would be a crime of blasphemy. While this is rarely a concern in the USA, a few states have blasphemy laws on the books, usually dating back a century or more. The state prosecuting such a law would likely see the case in the Supreme Court and the law struck down, but if you are planning a religious book bonfire, check the local laws, but especially the fire safety codes. Question: Why does Nikki Haley insist on continuing her campaign for the Republican nomination despite losing her home state of South Carolina to Donald Trump?
Answer: Believe it or not, most Presidential campaigns are not suspended when a candidate loses. Rather, they are suspended when a candidate runs low on money. Losing elections usually results in lowered donations, but the effect is indirect. The campaign continues as long as it’s funded, or there are other circumstances. When incumbent politicians run for President, they sometimes bow out early, with money, as their Presidential Campaign coffers can be directly transferred to their next run for Senate or Governor. Haley’s not looking for another office at present, so she lacks this motivation. Haley has been flush with cash, so no motivation to bow out yet. Both her campaign and the primary SuperPAC supporting her, SFA Fund, have received the support of traditional Republican megadonors. They have been supporting her, and have plans at present to support Trump. She's brought in donors who had been supporting Ron DeSantis and Mike Pence, among others. However, the SuperPAC kind of shot their wad in the last few months, spending $63 million to boost her profile, leaving only $3.5 million at present. Her campaign is much better off, but if donations dry up, expect it to be suspended. She’s announced that she’s sticking in until at least Super Tuesday (March 5th), which isn’t all that far off. Certainly because she's the last standing Trump opponent, but also because she would likely be a “normal" Republican. Stable leadership is better for business than a new Stupid Trump Trick every week. Big money people are not idiots, and don't just hand out money. They place their bets that a little money on a campaign yields a large benefit if the candidate's policies impact that person's fortunes, possibly more if it buys them specific future influence, of course. But it's money wasted if the candidate can't win. The big money knows Trump can't beat Biden, and will likely be a convicted felon by election day. They also know Trump will spend their donations on his legal defense, and he'll be mired in legal problems, rather than concentrating on the election. Haley polls much better against Biden, even though Trump is beating her in the primaries. So they're essentially betting, rather than take their toys, go home -- no value in supporting Trump, he will lose -- they'll try to keep Haley supported in the event Trump's whole campaign comes crashing down, which seems more likely every week. In fact, she outraised Trump in the last month, and spent much less. Trump spent far more than he brought in, including $2 million in legal expenses. Trump's grassroots supporters are tapped out and slowly but finally getting tired of paying his personal bills. It's also looking pretty likely that Trump's business fraud case will have exposed him as lying all these years about being a billionaire, in a way even the MAGAs may understand. However, this may not last. Just in the last day, one Republican megadonor network, Charles Koch’s donor network, Americans for Prosperity, has decided to drop support of Nikki Haley. Question: Which is better, a TV with a higher pixel count or one with a higher pixel density like a mobile device?
Answer: Unless you’re holding your television on your hand, you’re not buying on the basis of pixel density. First of all, while phones come in a wide variety of screen sizes and resolutions, TVs come in all sizes, but nearly all these days are either Full HD (1920x1080 pixels) or UltraHD-4K (3840x2160 pixels). Yes, there are very old displays at HD (1280x720) and some very high end models at UltraHD-8K (7680x4320 pixels), but I’m thinking that no one asking this question is looking at 8K screens. So pick high or low resolution, and within that resolution, screen size and pixel density are inversely proportional, but the ratio is unchanged. Thus, no one thinks about pixel density. If you’re buying a real 2024 vintage television (and I’m in the market, so I have been thinking about these things), your first consideration is your screen size. Here’s another useful area of consideration: you never worry about pixel density because you’ll never sit close enough to resolve individual pixels if you buy the right television. Your first move is to decide where the television goes and how far away you’ll be viewing from. This will suggest the smallest television that will give you the full resolution experience. Here’s a calculator to help with this. So I have a Livingroom awaiting delivery of a console my wife custom ordered… we’re expecting it early next month. This is going to put the television about 12ft from the couch. The other one goes in the Florida room. We don’t have a couch there yet, but I just completed some construction there (the room contained a hot water heater, washer, and dryer which are all now in my new laundry room) and left a nice hookup place for a new TV on the wall, about 9ft from where the couch goes. By this chart, the Livingroom TV should be 95″ and the Florida room TV should be And sure, opinions vary on resolution distance. Some charts and calculators claim if I’m 12ft away I’ll need about a 120″ television, but this one claims 85″ should be good. That’s might take some negotiations with the wife, but I’m confident I’ll get at least 75″ there. For the Florida room, the calculator recommends 65″ or better. That’ll be easy. There’s also another guideline which has nothing to do with resolution: optimal screen viewing angle. In short, how large should the TV be in your visual field for a good theatrical experience. Both THX and SMPTE have guidelines for this. For my Livingroom, a 75″ screen will give me a 25.6° viewing angle. The recommended SMPTE viewing distance would be 10.2ft for the preferred 30° viewing angle. The maximum THX viewing distance is 11.8ft, for a 26° viewing angle… pretty close. The optimal THX viewing angle is 36°. If I swapped that for an 85″ television, I’m still a bit short at 28.9° for optimal SMPTE viewing recommendations, but past the 26° minimum THX angle of view. In the Florida room, a 65″ television gets me a 29.4° field of view, close to nailing the SMPTE ideal spec, but still short of the THX ideal of 36°. If I bump that up to 75″ — maybe buy two of the same television for both rooms — I’m now at 33.7°, which is in excess of the SMPTE recommendation and not that far from the THX optimal. Again, this is out of concern for the screen size, not the screen resolution. I just happened to have notice awhile back that the recommended viewing distances for Ultra-4K displays are generally very close to the SMPTE/THX viewing distances visual field. Question: Will Nikon be able to crush Sony and Canon with their new acquisition of the Red Cinema cameras?
Answer: Nope. Of course, Red is a well-accepted Cinema camera company. They hit the ground running in 2007 with the Red One, one of the first cinema cameras with a Super35mm-sized sensor (think APS-C), a format in the same basic dimensions as 35mm film (ARRI pioneered this with the Arriflex D-20 in 2005). ShotOnWhat? lists 504 movies shot on Red cameras, which is a bit more than either Canon or Sony. Nikon was the only one of the three that didn’t offer Cinema cameras, or really, any camera for dedicated video. The big four in camcorders going back decades were Sony, Panasonic, JVC, and Canon, crossing from consumer to professional and, in some cases, into the modern world of digital cinema cameras. Canon’s been making pro-grade camcorders since the late 1980s, the days of analog Hi-8mm tape. Canon launched their Cinema EOS line of cinema cameras in 2011, naturally with an almost Super35mm-sized sensor, six years after Red was founded in 2005 (Canon used the same slightly smaller 24.6 x 13.8 mm “APS-C” sensor format they use in their stills cameras). Cinema EOS has been a direct competitor of Red. ShotOnWhat? lists 276 films shot on Canon cameras (all kinds). Sony introduced professional ENG camcorders to the market in 1982. They also lead the market for low-end professional camcorders, the sort used by professional event videographers, particularly with the immensely popular DCR-VX1000 (digital DV tape) in 1995, and even my first pro HDV camcorder, the HVR-A1 in 2006. Sony introduced their highly regarded CineAlta line of digital cinema cameras in 2000 with the HDW-F900R. Their first cinema cameras were based on the sensor technology from ENG models. Sony’s first Super35-sensor, PL-mount, $250,000 cinema camera was the F35, introduced in 2008. But just two years later, the hand-held, also PL-mount PMW-F3 was introduced for only $16,000. ShotOnWhat? lists 393 films shot on Sony (all kinds). Let’s get a little perspective here, too. Red made $159.2M in 2023… a nice business. Nikon’s 2023 revenue was $4.648 billion. Canon’s 2023 revenue was $30.04 billion, and Sony’s revenue was $88.97 billion. Yes, Canon and Sony are into many different markets and products. Nikon has some diversified businesses, too, so only $1.54 billion of that was their 2024 imaging division. But Sony made $3.83 in their cameras and audio division, even more in the semiconductor division, at $18.5 billion… including quite a few Nikon sensors. Canon claimed $5.8 billion revenue in their imaging division. However you slice it, the Red deal is just a drop in the bucket for Nikon in terms of existing revenue. But it’s presumably bringing Red’s technology into Nikon and expanding the reach of their overall business. You’ll find, while Red, Canon, and Sony do well, the big dogs in the cinema camera business are ARRI (1,927 films listed) and Panavision (1,556 films listed), but those are higher-end than Red, Canon, and Sony. And you can only rent a Panavision, never buy it. Read More

Question: Why do my camera photos look even worse than phone photos in terms of quality? For example, if I zoom in on my camera photo it looks blurry and then on my phone it has more details.
Answer: You didn’t mention the kind of camera you’re using. Something like this low-end Sony point-and-shoot model? Yeah, you can easily get a sharper image on a smartphone. This camera has a 20.1 megapixel sensor, as it tells you on the camera. It’s also starting out with an f/3.2 aperture on a 1/2.3″ sensor . That’s a very tiny sensor, much smaller than the sensor in any 2022–2024 premium smartphone. Thanks to diffraction — the bending of light passing though an aperture — you’re probably getting maybe an effective “optical” 10–12 megapixels at full aperture. Zoom all the way out and you’re at f/6.4. You’ll have less than 2 megapixels of optical resolution. In short, the image will be much blurrier than you’d like. With the smartphone, you’re probably getting 12–16 megapixels of actual resolution these days (some claim to have much more, but that’s not exactly correct), but you’ll have a larger sensor and probably be shooting at f/2.0-f/1.5 on the main camera. So no diffraction… you get a sharp image. The phone’s software is also shooting multiple images and merging them for less noise and better dynamic range, and then applying all kinds of sharpening and color modification — often too much — to deliver an image most novices, at least, will find pleasing. If your phone has a portrait or telephoto camera, you might about match the magnification of this camera at full zoom, but of course, your phone is doing with multiple cameras, each with a prime lens, and at least for premium models, increasingly not-terrible sensors and lenses. I did a review of the Honor Magic4 Pro awhile back, which offered a telephoto camera consisting of a 1/2.0″ sensor — largely than the Sony’s — and a 3x, f/2.0 lens. So immediately better than what you can get out of the Sony, probably even at a software-driven 5x magnification. And that’s a two-year-old smartphone! Maybe it’s more like this, a lower-end bridge camera? With this, you have exactly the same problem: a tiny 1/2.3″ sensor and relatively narrow aperture. This Panasonic probably does a bit better than the Sony on diffraction, with a slightly faster aperture range, but that’s probably negated by a lens that’s trying to deliver a 60:1 magnification range. Despite being made of plastic, your smartphone’s lens is going to be sharper. Today’s smartphone lenses are nearly all injection molded of optical plastic, but they’re pretty good at that these days, and they can fit a 6 or 7 element lens with the cheap ability to mold aspherical lens elements. Professional zoom lenses designed today can rival fixed-focus prime lenses, but a lens pushed to these limits, and made pretty cheaply as well, is not going to offer good sharpness. Now, of course, if you’re zoomed all the way in to 215mm on this camera, you’re at a full-frame equivalent of 1200mm… that’s nuts. You will get much better photos than your smartphone at that magnification level. Now, if you’re using a higher-end compact digital camera like this Sony RX100, you ought to be getting much better images than you do with your phone. Certainly sharper at just about any zoom level, because this camera has a 1″ sensor that’s not going to deliver diffraction at any magnification with full aperture, though you can stop down the aperture. This also shoots an honest 20 megapixels. Here’s another option that’ll outshoot your phone, the Sony RX10. This is a high-end bridge camera, and it’s got a 1″ sensor as well, in fact, probably the same one, depending on the RX100 model. And if you have one of these Digital Single Lens Reflex camera... … or one of these mirrorless interchangeable lens cameras, you ought to be getting better, sharper images than you do with your phone. So without knowing your specific case, if it’s any of these last groups, high-end compact digitals, DSLRs, or MILCs, you’re doing something wrong if your phone is delivering better images. So, since you didn’t really explain your situation, I tried to cover a range of cases. Hope that’s useful.

Eight states allow any election to be conducted entirely by mail, including California (2021), Colorado (2013), Hawaii (2019), Nevada (2021), Oregon (1988), Utah (2012), Vermont (2021). Washington (2011) and the District of Columbia (2022). Two more red states, Nebraska and North Dakota, leave it up to each country to decide if they want entirely mail-in elections. Alaska, Arizona, Florida, Kansas, Maryland, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico and Wyoming have large-scale mail-in voting and permit some elections to be held entirely by mail, and allow anyone to vote by mail without excuse. Additionally, Idaho, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Virginia, and Wyoming allow anyone to mail-in their vote, no special case needed. The only objection to mail-in voting came from Donald Trump because, as with everything else, he’s an idiot and doesn’t understand much of anything about anything. Question: My iPhone 12 Pro battery health has dropped to 91% in 8 months. It’s dropping by 1-2% every month. Should I be concerned?
Answer: It's entirely dependent on how many times you fully charge it. An iPhone battery is good for about 500 full charges. So if you run down to 0% each day, you can charge about 500 times before you need a new battery. If you put it on your power adapter at 50% charge each night, it should last 1,000 half charges. An LCO battery — by industry standard — is considered “used up” when it can only charge to 80% of the original charge level, which as said is after about 500 full charges. Doing that math, you can expect the battery “health" to drop by 1% every 25 full charges. Drop that bad boy on your power adapter near dead every night and you can certainly expect to lose a point or two each month. Some Li-ion formula, such as NMC, NCA, and LPF batteries have a longer cycle life, and are still reasonably viable when they’re down to 70% of their charge capacity. These are not used in portable electronics because they have a lower specific energy, and the big push among smartphone makers is device runtime, not battery longevity. You might note, if you followed the link, that Apple’s warranty is 500 cycles for iPhones for 1,000 cycles for everything else they make. They could be using alternate battery chemistries in iPads, MacBooks, and Apple Watches, or they could be short-cycling LCO batteries so they never charge beyond 80%. Most portable power tools use LMO batteries, which optimize specific power, not energy, and have a much shorter battery cycle life, probably around 300 cycles. Read More

Question: Is it realistic for tech companies to create a universal charger that works across devices and brands?
Answer: It is! For example, the various USB connectors have evolved to support just this. Originally delivering 2.5W power available for charging purposes — never enough — the USB specification has evolved through the Battery Charging specification — 7.5W, still not enough — to today’s Power Delivery specification, the most recent of which an support fast charging on phones all the way up to up to 240W for charging or powering high current devices like laptop and even small desktop computers. There’s just one catch: the thing everyone calls a “charger” isn’t a charger. It’s just a power supply. The more recent protocols makes it a smart power supply, sure, but it knows absolutely nothing about charging batteries. It offers somewhere between +5Vdc at 500mA and +48Vdc at 5A, depending on the version of the “charger” and the device it’s asked to power. What the powered device does with that power is up to the device, not the “charger.” This is the critical part of how USB is universal. The charger itself is embedded in any device that charges from a USB connector. That’s the second half of how it’s made universal. Your phone, your laptop, your camera, whatever is designed with a power management system and complete knowledge of its own charging needs. One additional aspect of this architecture is that, unlike the days of the dedicated power supply, a device connected to a USB power supply can’t necessarily rely on that power supply to provide enough power for its operation and charging. In the past, connecting a charger to your laptop might leave the battery completely unused except for charging purposes. Today, as it’s been for ages with smartphones, the device has to be designed to be able to use battery and external power at the same time when power loads get high, dropping back to charging when the loads drop.

Question: Why did NASA astronaut Don Pettit say that we don’t have the technology to go to the moon, that we destroyed it? What was he intimating?
Answer: So here’s Don Pettit: astronaut, chemical engineer PhD, renowned space photographer, and the first man to invent a thing in space and win a patent for it (the Zero Gravity Coffee Cup!). Dr. Pettit has logged more than 370 days in space and over 13 spacewalk hours. Like most astronauts, he’s a truly exceptional human being, and currently at 69 years old, the oldest serving astronaut at NASA. His actual quote: I'd go to the moon in a nanosecond. The problem is, we don't have the technology to do that anymore. We used to, but we destroyed that technology and it is a painful process to build it back again. So, maybe you need an engineer’s explanation… I volunteer (I’m also a photographer, but tragically, not an astronaut). What Don is referring to isn’t our simple lack of an Saturn V rocket, but rather, the loss of the system that delivers the parts to make additional rockets. NASA rockets are built by a hugely complex coordinated effort of hundreds if not thousands of private companies contracted by NASA to build the various components. But that’s really not the core of what he’s saying here, I believe. President Richard Nixon cancelled the last several Apollo missions in September of 1970, thus ending the production of new Saturn V super-heavy lift vehicles and other critical components. NASA still flew Apollo 16 and Apollo 17, both missions in 1972, but NASA had planned to fly though Apollo 20. So, lacking any orders for new Saturn V rockets from NASA and any likely possibility of such orders, all of those contractors who built the parts for Saturn V rockets started dismantling their production lines and repurposing them for something else. The same thing they do for any other contract project. It’s not as if NASA had a full soup to nuts Saturn V production line (they did final assembly) and sent Neil, Buzz, and all the boys down with sledgehammers to “Hulk Smash” the remnants of the Apollo program. I’m not pretending to speak for Dr. Pettit, but I have a pretty good idea that he was expressing his frustration in NASA’s directions, which were my frustrations as well, as a kid who grew up watching manned rockets take off and fly farther every time, only for all that to end before I could get involved. Astronauts fly to space, and so of course, as an astronaut, he was heartbroken by the end of travel to the Moon and beyond. Quite a few scientists, NASA and otherwise, love their probes and robots and don’t see so much value in manned travel, and so today we have Mars, a planet entirely occupied by robots. Had NASA been funded and, of course, permitted by the political winds to keep sending people up, we’d likely have humans there today. What he’s absolutely not suggesting is that you’d want Saturn V today, but rather, if the Apollo program had not been cancelled, if we had kept flying manned missions, the Saturn V would naturally have been replaced by improved rockets, and those replaced by the next generation. If you’ve seen the television show For All Mankind, that’s kind of the idea. The technology would have evolved faster and more cleanly than waiting 35 years to restart, and even at that by fits and sputters: Constellation, Asteroid Redirect Mission, Orion, and finally SLS and Artemis. But the Artemis I mission has flown around the Moon, and while it was unmanned, the SLS super-heavy lift vehicle did propel the Orion spacecraft that’s designed for humans to travel to the Moon and back. Artemis II is planned for sometime in or after September of 2025, with a crew: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen. The old is always “destroyed” to make way for the new. Ford lacks the technology to build a Model-T today. Intel lacks the technology to build an 8088 today. McDonnell-Douglas lacks the technology to build a DC-3 today. Those were single products, sure, but also product lines that were in continuous development and improvement. And still continues today. There was a Kickstarter project called Reflex launched in 2017, with the goal of creating a new fully manual, modular 35mm camera system. They last posted in 2021, discussing problems, then the apparent impossibility, of obtaining a mechanical focal plane shutter mechanism. That technology had been destroyed, and while they could manage other parts of the camera system, that was apparently beyond the capabilities of a small group like this. Pentax is supposedly working on a more modest compact film camera for release this year… maybe they’ll have better luck. But even existing camera companies didn’t simply have that technology lying around… I suspect they’ll adapt modern parts. The old stuff makes way for the new. That’s true of ideas, too, particularly those silly ideas of pre-scientific people that expired about 2,500 years ago, like “Flat Earth,” in the light of improved human knowledge. Question: Why did Intel discontinue the use of Pentium chips in laptops? Was it due to a decrease in performance or other reasons?
Answer: Intel released the first Pentium, also known as the i586, in 1993. This was Intel’s next major push both into technology but also into branding. Competitive x86 processors by then could also work a “5” or a “6” into their names, but they couldn’t copy Intel on a new brand for their product line. The Pentium brand persisted through the Pentium 2, Pentium 3, and Pentium 4 as Intel’s consumer flagship processor. However, the Pentium 4 had become a bit problematic. Dubbed the Netburst Architecture, this iteration pushed to very high clock speeds — clock speed had sadly become an important consumer metric in the marketplace — with super long pipelines, lots of power consumption, but little real improvement in performance. The Netburst Architecture proved very fast at some things, but basically, any time code didn’t run quite as expected, it took massive penalties thanks in a big part to the deep instruction pipeline: 20 stages in Willamette, 31 stages in Prescott. That’s versus 14 stages in the Pentium III and 12 in the AMD Athlon64 at the time. In addition, Intel had expected to keep tweaking up the clock speed — one of the main reasons for such a deep pipeline — but failed to really get there. Intel had initially claimed they’d get the Pentium 4 to 10GHz! They topped out at 3.8GHz. Did I mention the high power needed? In order to support laptops, Intel, specifically Intel Israel, proceeded along parallel lines and evolved the P6 architecture — specifically, the last version of the Pentium III — toward a lower power design, versus their previous process of evolving the high-end processor down for lower power use. This became the Pentium M in 2003. Which became a hit in tiny desktops and embedded processing in addition to the laptop use. As it turned out, this was a good move. Intel eventually introduced a whole new architecture, branded the Intel Core Architecture, as their replacement for the Pentium 4. Could they simply have called it Pentium 5? Of course, it’s only branding. But the Pentium 4 had seriously damaged Intel’s reputation. While they’re not brand new, the last versions of the Pentium are still available in off-the-shelf laptops. Intel has announced that they’re staring to phase out the Pentium and Celeron lines, but they have not yet at the time of this writing. This one, for example, the Lenovo IdeaPad 1 14IGL7. This incorporates the Intel Pentium Silver N5030, a four core processor running at a 1.1GHz base clock, with overclocking to 3.1GHz. The laptop contains 4GiB DRAM and 128GB of eMMC flash. It’s $185 on Amazon. Intel’s line, from top performance, on down, includes: Core i9 Core i7 Core i5 Core i3 Intel Processor Pentium Gold Pentium Silver Celeron Atom Intel is pushing the Pentium and Celeron lines into very low cost laptops, including Chromebooks. Some of these lower end processors also make sense in embedded applications, and that’s the only target for Intel’s Atom processors. They had a bit of a failure of their own when first sold into Intel’s NetBook concept. It’s pretty clear: Intel needs to stay far away from using the word net in any future products! Question: Why do citizen-led ballot initiatives face a steep path to getting on the ballot in Florida?
Answer: It’s not that hard to launch a ballot initiative in Florida. In fact, in any given year, Florida receives tens of thousands of ballot initiative petitions. Unlike some states, there is a defined process for this. The problem, as you might expect, is that there has to be some kind of threshold for these, or you’d have 100 pages of initiatives to sort through in every election. So it’s necessary, to get a ballot initiative to the point it’s actually going to get a popular vote, it’s necessary to get at least 8% of the total vote from the previous Presidential election in validated, signed petitions. That’s currently 877,263 petitions. That’s the easy part, and if there’s some very interested organization backing a ballot measure — all the serious ones have sponsors — with money to get the word out, it’s absolutely possible. Some of the petitions officially logged are over the required number of petitions, but have not necessarily been validated. Yeah, Florida has to validate every petition… I mean, it makes sense. Question: How much money does Donald Trump need to raise for the Republican National Committee?
Answer: There’s probably no mandatory number… other than “as much as possible,” when a Presidential candidate is raising money for their party committee. The Presidential candidate is always be best money attractor in a Presidential year, and they do typically fund the party pretty well. Why? party can make strategic donations to down-ballot campaigns. While of course each party wants to win an election, they also understand that winning the Presidency but losing both Houses of Congress basically gets us two years of stasis… nothing gets done. Since we all know Trump is among the greediest people walking planet Earth, and can only think transactionally, never strategically. let’s look at Joe Biden’s campaign first. Largely because of donation limit laws, there are multiple vehicles for donations. A donor can contribute directly to the Biden for President campaign. That money, as we’re still in the primary election despite the fact both Biden and Trump are shoe-ins at this point, up to $3,300 goes to Biden’s primary campaign, then the next $3,300 goes to Biden’s general election campaign. Any more would either have to be returned to the donor or redesignated to another fund, with the donor’s permission. You might expect that political campaigns hate to give money back, and that a smart Presidential campaign will understand the critical nature of keeping a financially sound party, both at the national and local level, and well funded down-ballot candidates. So lots of fundraising is done though pass through accounts. You give money to the pass-through, and it will apply the funds, usually following a set of rules for percentage distributions and dealing with overflows, to ensure the whole party makes the best use of the money being donated. In Biden’s case, there’s a passthrough called the Biden Victory Fund. This is pretty much the way the Democratic Party runs every Presidential election. In the 2024 cycle so far, the Biden Victory Fund has raised $159,605,099. The Biden for President campaign received $59,925,500 (37.5%), the Democratic National Committee received $15,500,000 (9.7%), 37,539,430 (23.5%) has yet to be allocated, and the remaining $46,590,169 (29.2%has gone to at least 43 state Democratic committees (Open Secrets). My recollection was that the National Party usually gets around 10%, and this seems on target. There was a Trump Victory Fund in 2016 and in 2020. There seems to have been $1,815,914 in this account left over from 2020 at the start of the 2024 election cycle. $509,180 of that was donated to “Make American Great Again PAC” which is one of several Trump Leadership PACs. Money in a Leadership PAC can’t be used for regular campaign expenses, but it can be used for practically anything else. It can be transferred to other candidates’ campaigns — that was the original purpose of the Leadership PAC: to allow party leaders to fund candidates they favored. This fund can also pay Trump’s legal expenses, pay for his vacation, pay him to “consult” for other campaigns, and practically anything else. It’s effectively his money. The main fundraising arm for Trump is Trump Save America JFC. This is a passthrough that sends 90% of the money collected to main campaign, Donald J. Trump for President primary campaign, and 10% to Save America, another Trump Leadership PAC. The wording of the site suggests that money over $3,300 donated would go first to Save America, which can accept $5,000 from an individual in any year, then on to the Trump Campaign’s general election fund. As well, they don’t have joint fundraising with the RNC or any other fund, so the donation limit is listed as $11,600. So Trump seems to be raising precisely zilch for the RNC. Now, it’s also true that political committees can directly fundraise. There’s a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee aggregating donation for House candidates, a Democratic Senate Campaign Committee which does the same for Senatorial candidates, and the Democratic National Committee itself. The three of these have collected a total of $352 million and paid out a total of $305 million in the 2024 election so far. The Republicans have the same three types of fundraising committees, which have brought in $288 million and paid out $257 million in the 2024 election cycle so far. So they have been raising money, just not without Trump’s help. In 2021, Trump advised his supporters to not fund the RNC, their Senate or House committees, or any other candidates directly, but to send it all to Trump (CNBC), and he doesn’t seem to have changed that attitude. So Trump’s campaign is largely small donor supported, while the Republican megadonors have largely steered clear of Trump, but are trying to make up the deficits the RNC has been suffering without help from their Presidential candidate. That was an unusual move, but even worse, Trump ordered the RNC to stop using his name and image in any of their fundraising. That may change this year, but not necessarily for the better. Trump just successfully ousted Ronna McDaniel from hearing the RNC, installing Michael Whatley, an election denier Trump hand picked to run the RNC, along with his daughter-in-law Lara, as the chair and vice-chair of the RNC. Lara Trump has already claimed that “every single penny” of RNC funds would go to Trump’s re-election. This apparently already includes paying Trump’s direct legal bills (they probably can’t pay his fines or judgements). So basically, Trump has completely reverse the usual campaign dynamic: he’s not raising money for the Republican National Committee. Every penny the RNC raises is now going to Donald Trump.
